verses.translation_literal: To the leader, with stringed instruments: a psalm, of Asaph, a song.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung with the strings: a psalm of Asaph, a song.
verses.directors_commentary: This is a stage direction, not part of the poem. In the Hebrew numbering the title counts as verse 1, which is why every verse below carries a number one higher than in the KJV. 'To the chief Musician' (לַמְנַצֵּחַ) names the temple music master who held the piece in his repertoire. The KJV's 'Neginoth' leaves the Hebrew untranslated as if it were a tune name. It is a plain plural of 'stringed music', and the ASV and YLT render it so. Both 'psalm' (מִזְמוֹר, a piece sung to plucked strings) and 'song' (שִׁיר) appear, so the piece is a cultic song with instruments. Asaph was a Levite singer of David's time and the head of a guild of temple singers who bore his name; the ל in 'of Asaph' may mean 'by', 'for' or 'in the manner of' the guild. Later readers tied the psalm to the Assyrian disaster under Hezekiah (Malbim on Ps 76:1). The Hebrew title says nothing of it.

philological_notes.note: A Piel participle with the article: 'the one who leads, the overseer', as the music master of the temple. The root also means 'to be eminent, to prevail', which explains the old rendering 'to the victor'.
A plural of 'stringed music', from the root 'to pluck strings'. It is not the name of a melody, which the KJV's untranslated 'Neginoth' suggests.

verses.translation_literal: Known in Judah [is] God; in Israel great [is] his name.
verses.translation_dramatic: In Judah, God is known. In Israel, his name is great.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem opens with two short lines in a parallel pair, and the first thing to hear is the order: the verb 'known' stands first and the divine title last. God has been seen in what he did, so the line is a report of an event rather than a creed. The KJV's 'In Judah is God known' is accurate, but its added 'is' loses the Hebrew's blunt verb-first start. Note also the verb form: נוֹדָע is a Niphal participle, 'made known, shown', not 'recognized'. Judah and Israel are not two enemies here. Commentators read them as the south and the whole people, with Judah first for the royal tribe (Meiri on Ps 76:2), or as Jerusalem's inhabitants and the rest of the tribes (Ibn Ezra, Malbim). The word used for God is 'Elohim', which is why this section of the Psalter, the Elohistic Psalter, avoids the name YHWH until verse 12. The 'name' in ancient Near Eastern speech is a reputation that others have heard of, not a label.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle of 'to know': 'is made known, is revealed', and so not 'is merely recognized'. Ibn Ezra compares 'for David was made known' for the same verb form.

verses.translation_literal: And it was in Salem, his booth, and his dwelling in Zion.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so his shelter was set in Salem, and his dwelling place on Zion.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Salem' is the short, older name of Jerusalem, as in Genesis 14:18 where Melchizedek is king of Salem (Metzudat Zion on Ps 76:3), and it puns on 'shalom', peace. The poet uses it here so that peace is in the city's name just before the war language of verse 4. Radak adds a midrash that God merged Abraham's 'Yireh' and Shem's 'Salem' to make 'Yerushalayim'. The KJV's 'tabernacle' is a Latin word that suggests the Mosaic tent. The Hebrew is סֻכּוֹ, 'his booth, his thicket', a word used elsewhere for a lion's covert (Ps 10:9; Jer 25:38). Its pair, מְעוֹנָתוֹ, is 'his lair, his den' (Nah 2:12; Ps 104:22). The poet very likely wants an animal undertone to prepare verse 5's 'mountains of prey', so that God is a lion who lairs on Zion. This is my own reading, not the commentators'. The opening 'and it was' has no English equivalent. The KJV's 'also' is an addition that the Hebrew does not have.

philological_notes.note: 'His booth, his covert'; elsewhere the lair of a lion (Ps 10:9; Jer 25:38). Malbim reads it as a temporary dwelling, set against 'mĕ'onah' as a fixed one. The lion reading is mine, hence the sources below cover only the other points.
Salem, the old name of Jerusalem (Gen 14:18), and a word of the same root as 'peace'.

verses.translation_literal: There he broke the flashes of the bow, shield and sword and battle. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: There he snapped the fiery flights of the bow, the shield, the sword, the whole of war. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: 'There' (שָׁמָּה) points back to Zion. It is the poem's pivot, with the vowel-ending he marking motion, 'to there', as if the arrows flew toward the city and were broken at its edge. The Hebrew for arrows is רִשְׁפֵי־קָשֶׁת, literally 'sparks, flames of the bow'. The KJV flattens this to 'arrows of the bow'. Resheph is also the name of a Canaanite plague and war god, and the word elsewhere means a burning thing (Song 8:6; Hab 3:5). To say that YHWH 'broke the flames of the bow' is a pointed insult to a god of fiery plague, and the war god is made a weapon that the true God snaps. The pe in this word is soft, as Rashi and Meiri stress, against the hard pe of 'flames of fire' in Song 8:6, so the old grammarians argued that the sense is 'flying things'. 'Shield, sword and battle' come as a list without verbs; the last item, 'battle', is the surprise, since a battle is not an object you can break, and the poem breaks it anyway. Selah is probably a pause or an instrumental interlude. Its exact sense is lost.

philological_notes.note: 'Flashes, sparks'; the same word as the fire-spirit Resheph in Job 5:7 and Deut 32:24. Rashi and Meiri take 'resheph of the bow' as the arrows themselves, because they fly like sparks.
A musical or liturgical mark of uncertain meaning, most likely a pause or interlude. Malbim reads it as 'the end of the matter'.

verses.translation_literal: Light-filled [are] you, majestic, from [the] mountains of prey.
verses.translation_dramatic: You are radiant, LORD, ablaze with light, and terrible in your majesty: mightier than the mountains of prey, those high dens where the hunters crouch and tear.
verses.directors_commentary:
Play this as a shout of recognition after the broken weapons of the verse before. Two things are said of God: he is lit from within (נָאוֹר, from the root of 'light') and he is אַדִּיר, 'majestic, mighty', a word used of great waters and great kings. The KJV fuses them into 'glorious and excellent', and 'glorious' drops the light that opens the line.

The last phrase is the hard one, because Hebrew מִן can mean 'than' or 'from'. The KJV, Rashi (stronger than the tall, predatory giants) and Metzudat David (stronger than the mountains where the beasts of prey live) take it as a comparison, as the KJV's 'more ... than' shows. The ASV's 'from the mountains of prey' takes it as a source, and so do Radak and Meiri, who picture the lion coming out of the hills where it dens to hunt; Malbim adds that this lion comes out by night, and that the lion is the Lord going out from Zion against the camp of Assyria. In the ancient world a high place was where the predator, or the plundering army, had its lair and its stronghold, so the line says that the God of Zion is greater than every stronghold of violence. The BBE's 'eternal mountains' does not translate the Hebrew words of this verse, and I have not followed it.

philological_notes.note: A niphal participle of the root 'light': one lit up, radiant. Rashi instead derives it from נאר (as in 'he spurned his sanctuary', Lam 2:7) and reads 'you who strew your enemies'; Meiri records the same view as a minority. The first reading keeps the light; the second makes the word a verdict on enemies.

'Mountains of prey': the root means to tear, as a predator tears its kill. Radak says the hills where the beasts of prey dwell are called this; Rashi reads it as predatory giants as high as mountains; Metzudat David takes it as a figure for the army of Sennacherib.

verses.translation_literal: They were plundered, the mighty of heart; they slumbered their sleep; and not found, all the men of strength, their hands.
verses.translation_dramatic: The brave of heart lie stripped. They have slept their sleep, the long one, and not a man of might among them can find his own hands.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the aftermath, quiet and a little grotesque. The soldiers are called 'mighty of heart', and in Hebrew the heart is the seat of nerve and will, so these are the men who did not know fear. Now they are stripped, and asleep, and the sleep is the end of them: Meiri hears in 'their sleep' the eternal sleep of Jer 51:39, the sleep of death, and Radak says they were as good as dead, unable to fight. Metzudat David reads the same, that all lay as corpses.

The KJV is faithful here: it keeps the cognate accusative, 'slept their sleep' (נָמוּ שְׁנָתָם), which is in the Hebrew, and it keeps the bodily idiom 'found their hands'. Say that line slowly, because it is the most vivid in the verse: the strong men look for their hands and the hands are not there, which means that the arm that was to draw the bow no longer answers (Rashi glosses it as 'their strength'; Malbim says they lost their hands). The one real puzzle is the first verb. אֶשְׁתּוֹלְלוּ has an aleph where a hithpolel should have he; Rashi and Ibn Ezra explain it so, and Rashi ties it to שׁוֹלָל, the stripped, befuddled state of those led away fools (Job 12:17), while Radak ties it to שָׁלָל, 'spoil', so that they became the booty. The KJV's 'are spoiled' takes the second; the YLT 'spoiled themselves' sits between them. The BBE's 'wealth' is a paraphrase of that same root. In your playing, give the word both meanings: stripped and made fools of.

philological_notes.note: A rare form with aleph in place of the he of the hithpolel. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as a reflexive of 'to be foolish, stripped'; Radak takes it from 'spoil': they became plunder. Both senses suit the scene.
A cognate pair, 'slumbered their slumber'. The verb is the rarer, poetic one for sleep (Rashi relates it to תְּנוּמָה, 'slumber'). Meiri hears the sleep of death, with Jer 51:39.
'Did not find their hands': an idiom for being unable to use one's strength, most of all in fighting. Rashi reads 'their strength'; Radak 'to fight'.

token_glosses.gloss: they were plundered / made fools of

verses.translation_literal: From your rebuke, God of Jacob, [were] dead asleep, both chariot and horse.
verses.translation_dramatic: At your rebuke, God of Jacob, they sank into a stupor, chariot and horse together.
verses.directors_commentary: The cause is named: 'rebuke' (גְּעָרָה). The word is the shout a master uses to a beast, and the same noun is what God hurls at the sea and the chaos waters (Ps 18:16; 104:7). It is a command with force, not the KJV's mild 'rebuke' of the pulpit. The 'God of Jacob' answers the 'Israel' of verse 2: the same people, now with their ancestor's name, the underdog patriarch. The verb is נִרְדָּם, the heavy sleep that fell on Adam (Gen 2:21) and on Jonah in the hold of the ship, a sleep of helplessness, not of rest. It is singular because the whole army is seen as one body (Ibn Ezra reads it as 'each one'). 'Chariot' (רֶכֶב) is the chariot corps, the war machine of the age: the KJV's 'both the chariot and horse' is fair, and the YLT's 'rider' is not. Chariots and horses were what a king of the period boasted of, and the poem has them lie like stunned animals. The idea that the whole force simply stopped, without a blow, is the climax of the section.

philological_notes.note: A rebuke or war-cry spoken to a force. It is God's word of command over the sea (Ps 104:7) and over enemies. Here the rebuke alone is enough to stop the army.

A heavy, deep sleep, as in Gen 2:21 and Jonah 1:5. It is singular for a compound subject. Ibn Ezra takes it as 'each of the men of strength'; Rashi and Meiri call the waw of 'and chariot' redundant, like 'and Ayah' in Gen 36:24.

verses.translation_literal: You, fearful [are] you; and who will stand before you from the time of your anger?
verses.translation_dramatic: You. You are the one to fear. And who could stand in front of you, once your anger has been loosed?
verses.directors_commentary: The doubling 'You, to be feared, you' (אַתָּה נוֹרָא אַתָּה) is a pointing finger, and the KJV's 'Thou, even thou' captures the stress. Ibn Ezra says the repeat means 'you alone' (Ibn Ezra on Ps 76:8). The adjective is נוֹרָא, 'awesome, terrible', from the same root as 'fear', and the cluster of 'fear' words (נוֹרָא here, 'feared' in verse 9, 'the fearsome one' in verse 12) is what holds the poem together. KJV's 'ought to be feared' in verse 12 is an interpretive stretch; the Hebrew says simply 'the fearsome'. The KJV's 'when once thou art angry' is smooth but loses the sense of 'from then' (מֵאָז): the question is 'who stands from the moment your nose flares', which Rashi and Radak read as 'from the instant you grow angry'. The Hebrew word for anger is 'nose' (אַף), the flaring nostril of the angry animal, and the soldier who stands his ground is the person who has never seen it.

philological_notes.note: 'From the time of your anger', 'from the moment of your wrath'. Literally 'from then, your nose', since אַף is both 'nose' and 'anger'.

verses.translation_literal: From heaven you made judgment heard; earth feared and was quiet.
verses.translation_dramatic: From heaven you let your verdict sound. The earth heard it, and shrank, and fell silent.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem cuts from the battlefield to the cosmos. The verb 'made heard' (הִשְׁמַעְתָּ) is a causative: God does not merely speak, he makes the sentence audible to all. The KJV's 'Thou didst cause judgment to be heard' is correct. The word דִּין is the verdict of a court, a legal word: the scene is a trial, with the sentence read from the bench of heaven. The two verbs that follow, 'feared' and 'was still', form a pair of opposites. Fear usually brings noise and flight, and here it brings silence. In the ancient world a 'quiet' earth (שָׁקְטָה) meant peace, the land at rest after war, as in Judges 3:11, so the fear is the beginning of the poem's peace. Commentators vary as to what the earth is: Radak and Metzudat David make it the nations around, who stopped their wars, and Ibn Ezra reports that some read 'earth feared' as the wicked and 'was still' as the righteous.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'to hear': 'you made a verdict heard', a court sentence announced from heaven. Rashi ties it to Isaiah's prophecy against Sennacherib.

verses.translation_literal: When arose for the judgment God, to save all [the] humble of [the] earth. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: When God rose up to judge, it was to save, to save every humble soul on the earth. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse turns on a verb of posture. In the ancient courtroom the judge sat to hear a case, and rising was the move to act; so 'when God rose for judgment' is the moment the verdict becomes rescue, and the infinitive 'to save' says what the rising was for. Judgment here is not a threat but a deliverance, which is why the earth fell silent in verse 9.

The weight lies on עַנְוֵי־אָרֶץ. The KJV, the ASV and Webster have 'the meek', the YLT 'the humble', and the BBE 'the poor'. 'Meek' is the weakest of these for a modern ear, because it now suggests mildness and docility; the Hebrew is about people bowed down by those who have power over them (BDB: poor, afflicted, humble). Two ways to hear 'all the humble of the earth' are open. One is universal: whoever on earth is oppressed (Metzudat David: all the humble of the earth for ever, and the wicked will fear to harm them; the Targum has the righteous saying that God will rise to judge the wicked and rescue all the humble of the land for ever). The other is particular: Radak says Israel are the humble of the earth, rescued from the nations, and Rashi names Hezekiah and his company. The Hebrew allows both, so keep the word wide and let the audience hear Jerusalem in it. Selah is a pause or lift in the music, not a word to be spoken; the KJV prints it as if it were text.

philological_notes.note: 'The humble of the earth': those who are poor, afflicted and bowed down, not simply gentle. Radak identifies them with Israel; Metzudat David and the Targum read it of all who are humble, for ever; Rashi says Hezekiah and his company.
A musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or lift. It is not in the commentaries on this verse; the reading is my own.

verses.translation_literal: For [the] fury of man will praise you; [the] remnant of furies you will gird on.
verses.translation_dramatic: Even the rage of men will end by praising you. And what rage is left over, you will wear like a belt.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hardest line of the psalm, and the KJV buries the difficulty. 'Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee' is the familiar form, and the Hebrew supports it: the word translated 'wrath' (חֵמָה) is a hot fury, and 'praise' (תּוֹדֶךָּ, from the root of 'to give thanks') is the opposite. The idea is that human rage, however fierce, ends up giving God a victory he did not need to fight for. The second line is the trouble. 'You will gird on' (תַּחְגֹּר) is what a soldier does with a belt or a sword, as in the phrase 'gird on your sword'. The KJV's 'restrain' is a guess supported by a late Mishnah use (Rashi cites Bekhorot 37b); the ASV's 'gird upon thee' stays with the Hebrew picture. The picture is of God strapping on, as an ornament or a weapon, whatever fury is left over, so that nothing is wasted. 'Remnant' (שְׁאֵרִית) is the word of the prophets for the survivors, so the line may also hear the survivors of the proud. The plural 'furies' (חֵמֹת) follows 'fury' in the singular, setting one man's anger against many. Rashi gives both readings, 'you restrain' and 'you wear'. Malbim reads it with Sennacherib's anger, which God kept in check by a limit.

philological_notes.note: A Hiphil of 'to praise, to give thanks', with the suffix 'you'. Radak adds the sense 'against their will', and so human wrath ends in confession.

'You will gird on' (put on as a belt), from the noun for a belt. KJV and Webster's 'restrain' is a different sense, 'hold back', that Rashi supports from a Mishnah (Bekhorot 37b). Rashi also gives the 'belt' sense.

verses.translation_literal: Vow and pay to YHWH your God, all around him; let them bring a gift to the Fearsome One.
verses.translation_dramatic: Make your vows, and keep them, to the LORD your God. And let all who stand about him bring their gifts to the One who is to be feared.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem ends with a summons to the audience, and the register shifts from narrative to liturgy: this is the moment when the congregation is told to act. A vow (נֶדֶר) was a promise made in the hour of danger, such as 'if you save me, I will give an offering', and it had to be paid once the danger passed (Ps 66:13-14; Eccl 5:3-4). The command 'vow and pay' means 'keep your promises now that you have been rescued'. 'All around him' (כָּל־סְבִיבָיו) can mean the neighbors of Jerusalem, the surrounding nations (Radak on Ps 76:12, Metzudat David) or the angels about the throne; the KJV's 'that be round about him' leaves it open. The 'gift' (שַׁי) is tribute, the offering a vassal brings to a king, which is why this word is chosen: the nations that once sent tribute to Assyria are told to send it to the Fearsome One instead (Malbim reads it exactly so). The KJV's 'him that ought to be feared' adds an 'ought' that is not in the Hebrew. The noun מוֹרָא means 'the fear' itself or 'the object of fear', and Isaiah 8:13 calls God by it: 'let him be your fear'. This is the first and only point in the psalm where the name YHWH appears.

philological_notes.note: A gift or tribute brought to a superior; the nations bring it to a king. Malbim hears an implied contrast with the tribute paid to Assyria.
'To the Fearsome One': a title of God. Ibn Ezra and Meiri compare Isa 8:13, 'he is your fear'. The KJV's 'him that ought to be feared' puts in an 'ought'.

verses.translation_literal: He cuts off [the] spirit of rulers; awesome to [the] kings of [the] earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: He plucks the spirit from princes as grapes are plucked from the vine, and the kings of the earth look on and fear him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on a short, hard line, and its last word is a reprise. The root 'to fear' has run through the poem: 'you are to be feared' (v. 8), 'the earth feared' (v. 9), 'to the one to be feared' (v. 12), and now 'awesome to the kings of the earth'. The KJV scatters it among 'feared', 'feared', 'ought to be feared' and 'terrible'; and 'terrible' is archaic English for 'awe-inspiring', which to us sounds like a bad review. Keep one word, 'awesome' or 'feared', and say it each time the same way.

The first verb is וִבְצֹר, from the root of the grape harvest: to cut off the clusters. Ibn Ezra reads it so and glosses it 'cuts off'; Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Meiri read the other sense, 'to restrain, diminish' (as in Gen 11:6, 'nothing will be withheld from them'). The KJV 'cut off' is sound; what it loses is the picture, the vintager's pruning knife at work on rulers. 'Spirit' (רוּחַ) is the temper and pride of a ruler, his haughtiness; the Targum renders it 'the haughtiness of the spirit of the rulers'. 'Rulers' (נְגִידִים) are commanders and princes, the men who lead armies, so the line is about armies and their leaders.

Who are they? The traditional reading ties the whole psalm to the fall of Sennacherib's army outside Jerusalem. Rashi says so at verse 9 and Metzudat David at verses 6, 9 and 12, and Malbim takes this verse in particular as about the princes of Assyria and Sennacherib himself, whose spirit the Lord reduces. Radak records two views: in his Michlol, under חגר, he read the psalm of the camp of Assyria, but he now prefers to read it of Gog and Magog, because of the psalm before it; Meiri allows that as well and calls it the correct one for the same reason. Either way the point for the actor is the same: the proud who frightened the world are themselves frightened.

philological_notes.note: The root of the vintage (בָּצִיר): to cut off grapes, hence to cut off, cut down. Ibn Ezra reads it so; Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Meiri read 'to restrain, to diminish', as in Gen 11:6 and Job 42:2.
'The spirit of rulers': their pride, their temper. Rashi and the Targum read haughtiness of spirit; Metzudat Zion reads anger and pride.
'One to be feared', a niphal participle of the same root as 'feared' in verses 8, 9 and 12. The poem closes on the word it keeps repeating.
